prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map places the camera wearer’s hands and forearms nearest, roughly 0.2–0.6 m away, with the work surface and small craft object around 0.5–1 m away and the upper background generally farther, about 1–2 m. Across frames 1–3, both hands remain close together in front of the wearer and above the table; in frame 4 a forearm fills much of the foreground as the viewpoint turns, while in frame 5 a hand remains near the upper-right foreground and the other is out of view. The scissors and glue gun lie beyond the hands on the tabletop, approximately 0.7–1.2 m from the camera and within extended arm’s reach, with nearer arms intermittently occluding the table and craft piece. Compared with RGB, the map makes foreground-to-background ordering and the arms’ proximity clearer, but its distances are only rough: object boundaries bleed together, dark holes appear around occlusions, and the rotated fourth frame has particularly inconsistent background depth.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map mainly separates visible human skin from the tabletop and occasionally isolates objects such as the scissors, helping show that the large foreground regions are hands or forearms positioned in front of and partly covering the workspace. In frames 1–3, human regions enter from the lower left and lower right and meet near the center; by frame 4 a large arm crosses the central foreground, and in frame 5 only a right-side hand/forearm region is clearly visible while much of the scene is unlabelled. The labelled scissors sit above and to the right of the hands, about 0.3–0.6 m from them on the table and roughly 0.7–1.2 m from the camera; other tabletop items are partly masked, merged into surrounding regions, or outside the strip boundaries. This map is highly unreliable spatially because large parts of the table are labelled “person,” the same surfaces change colour between frames, and labels such as “mouse” and “tie” appear inconsistent with the RGB; it also cannot establish gaze, facing direction, or metric distance.
descriptions.pose: The pose map shows articulated hand keypoints, making finger orientation, hand separation, and overlap easier to see than in RGB, but it contains no usable yellow body skeletons. Two hands are detected in frames 1–3 at roughly the same depth and about 0.1–0.3 m apart, positioned centrally in front of the wearer; their keypoints draw closer and overlap near the center by frame 3, consistent with the hands approaching the same small object. Frame 4 contains one compact, partly overlapping hand configuration near the lower centre-right after the camera/viewpoint turns, while frame 5 shows a single hand near the upper right and leaves the other hand undetected or out of view. The hands appear within the camera wearer’s arm reach at about 0.2–0.6 m, but the map provides no dependable object distances, person-to-person spacing, body facing, or gaze, and several missing or crossed finger joints make exact orientation uncertain.
